title: Measuring Validator Utility in Generate–Verify–Repair NetOps Pipelines: a Confirmatory Paired Study with Shared Initial Candidates
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to test whether a multi-dimensional validator metric suite predicts end-to-end agentic NetOps success better than a single raw verifier pass rate. Using a synthetic intent→configuration task generator and a hosted generate–validate–repair (GVR) adapter under shared_initial_candidate semantics, we ran 200 paired tasks (baseline single-shot validity vs. final guarded validity after deterministic validation/repair) with gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses). All 200 baseline initial candidates were judged valid by the deterministic validator and no repairs were applied; guarded outcomes therefore matched baseline: baseline success = 200/200, guarded success = 200/200, paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI 0.00–0.00, exact McNemar p = 1.0). Confirmatory hypothesis H1 (expected guarded > baseline by 10 percentage points) was not supported. We report the preregistered methodology, execution manifest, exact analysis results, and a discussion that interprets this null outcome in context: (1) the shared_initial_candidate design implies the comparison tests validator-triggered downstream repair utility only (not independent generation differences), (2) the synthetic task generator and generator settings produced already-valid candidates for this model/seed set, and (3) the deterministic validator exercised mechanically checkable constraints but does not guarantee detection of semantic/intent misalignment. We present limits on external validity and propose next-step experiments: richer fault injection, multiple models and stochastic sampling, and explicit evaluation of validator coverage for semantic intent preservation. All artifacts, task manifests, and the immutable master-prompt reference are recorded in the execution bundle.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into executable network configurations and to automate NetOps workflows. Prior work proposes interposing deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to bound stochastic generation and produce verifiable outputs. However, the operational utility of validator metric suites (coverage, false-positive/false-negative rates, detection latency) for predicting end-to-end agent success has seen limited controlled, preregistered evaluation. Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment asking: does a multidimensional validator metric suite explain more variance in end-to-end task success than a single verifier pass rate? Our contribution is a closed, artifact-grounded confirmatory study with (i) a machine-readable preregistration, (ii) deterministic shared_initial_candidate paired design that isolates validator/repair effects (baseline single-shot validity vs guarded final validity after validation/repair), (iii) exact execution and analysis artifacts, and (iv) an evidence-grounded interpretation of a null confirmatory result together with prioritized next experiments.
sections.related_work: Existing literature motivates GVR and validator layers for reducing stochastic-code/configuration defects and for providing verifier-guided repair feedback [1]. Benchmarks for NetOps/AIOps show substantial failure modes in realistic troubleshooting and ticketing scenarios and emphasize ticket noise and false-premise robustness as important gaps [2],[3]. Other recent work designs self-healing orchestrators and auditable decision traces to reduce silent tool-driven failures in agentic systems [4]. Our study directly targets an empirical gap identified across these works: quantifying validator coverage and its predictive value for end-to-end guarded success under controlled, preregistered conditions.
sections.methodology: Design summary. Confirmatory paired design, preregistered study AC-2026-03. Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model: gpt-5-mini (provider openai_responses). Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate (exactly one initial sampled candidate per task was reused across baseline and guarded conditions). Important preregistered detail: temperature was recorded as null/unset in the archived model_configuration; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0. The preregistration explicitly fixed task indices, task_count=200, and planned_episode_count=400 (baseline+guarded). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Inclusion/exclusion rules and contamination procedures were preregistered. Task bank. We used a synthetic intent→configuration generator family (intent_configuration_repair_v1) producing challenging workflows (difficulty levels 'very_hard' to 'extreme') with explicit allowed-field constraints and required sequences. Validator and scoring. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed full intent-constraint validation and produced binary validity scores; validator traces include parsed command counts, required command counts, and violation codes. Execution contract and sampling. The adapter performed exactly one initial generation per task (initial_generation_calls_per_task=1) shared across conditions; maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. The execution manifest and raw outputs are archived and referenced below. Analysis. Primary test: paired analysis of binary success using the registered paired-permutation/McNemar routine with bootstrap (10,000 resamples) for CI estimation. Secondary analyses (registered but exploratory in this run) included per-validator FP/FN rates and detection-latency summaries.
sections.results: Execution summary. Run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count=400, completed_episode_count=400, model_calls_used=200 (one shared initial generation per pair), failed_episode_count=0. Key outcome (confirmatory): baseline_success_count = 200/200, guarded_success_count = 200/200. Paired contingency: n_11=200, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0; paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). Validator/repair behavior. For every task the validator trace records valid=True and repair_applied=false; no repair prompts were issued or used because the shared initial candidates already satisfied the validator's intent-constraint checks. Secondary metrics. Because all episodes were valid and un-repaired, per-validator FP/FN/latency distributions are degenerate in this dataset (no false negatives or false positives observed). Representative artifacts. We publish representative per-episode responses, validator traces, and the execution manifest paths (examples included in the archived bundle).
sections.discussion: Interpretation of confirmatory null result. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the experiment isolates downstream validator/repair utility: baseline measures the initial candidate's single-shot validity, guarded measures final validity after any permitted validator-triggered repair. The observed null effect arises because the initial candidates produced by gpt-5-mini for the selected synthetic tasks and seeds were already valid with respect to the deterministic validator's mechanically checkable intent-constraints. Scientifically this outcome limits the ability to evaluate validator-driven repair benefit in this run; it does not falsify the general value of validators but emphasizes that their measured utility depends on (a) the difficulty/fault-injection rate in the task bank, (b) the generator sampling regime, and (c) validator coverage (mechanically checkable vs semantic intent preservation). Implications for validator evaluation. A validator that is complete for a class of mechanically checkable violations can produce zero downstream repairs when generators already meet those constraints; measuring validator coverage therefore requires fault-injection targeted at classes the validator purports to detect. Future experiments should (i) inject synthetic semantic and configuration-logic faults that pass syntactic checks but violate intent, (ii) use stochastic generation (multiple sampled initial candidates per task) to measure variability, and (iii) test multiple model families and validator implementations to estimate external validity. Confirmatory vs exploratory results. The primary confirmatory hypothesis H1 (expected 10pp guarded improvement) was not supported. Exploratory questions about which fault classes drive FP/FN tradeoffs remain unanswered in this execution and are recommended for follow-up.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired study that operationalizes the question of whether a multidimensional validator metric suite predicts end-to-end guarded success better than a single verifier pass rate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the specific synthetic task bank, gpt-5-mini initial candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in every case; consequently no repairs were applied and guarded outcomes equalled baseline (200/200 successes). This null confirmatory result highlights three practical lessons: (1) shared_initial_candidate experiments test validator-triggered downstream repair utility, not generator differences; (2) validator utility can be masked when initial candidates are high-quality for the validator's mechanistic checks; (3) rigorous validator evaluation requires targeted fault injection and varied generator sampling. We therefore recommend next-step confirmatory runs with explicit, preregistered fault classes and multi-sample generation to meaningfully estimate validator FP/FN rates and the predictive power of validator metric vectors for operational-impact proxies. All execution artifacts and the master-prompt reference cited in the Disclosure Statement are archived with this manuscript.

limitations: Confirmatory scope was constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics: baseline and guarded conditions used the exact same initial generated candidate; only downstream validator/repair could create outcome differences.
The task bank was synthetic; while designed to be challenging ('very_hard'/'extreme'), it does not equal real production heterogeneity (multi-vendor devices, live ticket noise).
Single-model experiment: only gpt-5-mini was used. No multi-model generality claims are made.

No repairs were applied because all initial candidates passed the deterministic validator; therefore the study could not estimate repair effectiveness or validator false-negative behavior in this execution.

Validator scope: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces mechanistic intent-constraint checks but does not guarantee detection of semantic intent misalignment that is correct-by-structure but incorrect-by-intent.

Temperature=null in model configuration is recorded but does not imply deterministic sampling; execution sampling randomness and provider-side behavior may vary across calls and is documented in the manifest but not controlled to a fixed numeric temperature.

External validity: the results do not imply that GVR pipelines lack value generally; they show that, for this generator+model+task set under shared_initial_candidate semantics, validator-triggered repair was not invoked.
